analysis.one_liner: Forces federal approval of the Keystone XL oil pipeline from Canada to the Gulf Coast.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Lugar with 40 cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar, but was never voted on, and Congress adjourned without passing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the President to approve the Keystone XL pipeline permit within 60 days, unless the President formally found the pipeline was not in the national interest and reported why to Congress. If the President did nothing, the permit would take effect automatically. It also would have let Nebraska's governor submit a new in-state route to avoid the environmentally sensitive Sand Hills region, with that route automatically approved if the President did not act within 10 days.
analysis.who_benefits: The pipeline company and Canadian oil sands producers would gain a legislatively guaranteed permit and a guaranteed route decision, with environmental review declared complete and no further federal review allowed. Gulf Coast refiners would gain a new supply of heavy Canadian crude, and construction workers would gain temporary pipeline-building jobs. Nebraska would gain the ability to reroute the line away from the Sand Hills, but only through the governor's submission, not through new federal environmental review.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil sands producers and the pipeline company

how_it_helps.text: It would have forced approval of the permit for the pipeline carrying up to 830,000 additional barrels per day of crude (including 700,000 barrels per day of added Keystone system capacity) from Canada to Gulf Coast refineries.

It set a 60-day fuse: if the President neither approved the permit nor formally determined the pipeline was not in the national interest, the permit would take effect automatically by operation of law.

It offered a concession to opponents of the original route by allowing Nebraska's governor to submit an alternate route through the state, which would be deemed approved if the President did not act within 10 days.

analysis.who_pays: Landowners and communities along the pipeline route, especially in Nebraska's Sand Hills over the Ogallala aquifer, would bear the spill and water-contamination risk, since the bill barred any further federal environmental review. The broader public would bear the environmental cost of entrenching oil sands development, and the President would lose the authority to weigh the project's merits on the normal schedule.

drawbacks.text: The bill declared the completed environmental review sufficient and barred any further federal environmental review, eliminating the normal opportunity to reconsider based on new information or a changed route.
If the President did nothing within 60 days, the permit would take effect automatically, meaning the default outcome was approval rather than a considered decision.

The route through Nebraska would be chosen by the state's governor, with the route deemed approved if the President did not act within 10 days—removing federal authority over the most environmentally sensitive part of the route, the Sand Hills region.

Supporters' job-creation figures (around 20,000 direct jobs) were disputed at the time; independent estimates put permanent operating jobs far lower, and the main guaranteed beneficiaries were the pipeline company and oil producers, not long-term workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits—construction jobs, possible fuel-supply certainty—were real but modest and mostly short-term; the costs—foreclosing environmental review of a major oil-sands pipeline and overriding the normal presidential permitting process—were significant and long-lasting. Its centerpiece, a deemed approval by default if the President did nothing, shifted the burden so that inaction would have built the pipeline. The Nebraska rerouting provisions were the one part that responded to genuine local concerns, but the bill removed the federal government's ability to say no to the project overall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up for a vote, and when Congress ended in January 2013 it died; a similar deadline attached to the December 2011 payroll tax deal instead led President Obama to reject the pipeline permit in January 2012.

narrative.text: Senator Lugar introduced the bill on November 30, 2011 with 40 cosponsors (39 Republicans, 1 Democrat), and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on December 1, 2011.
No further action was ever taken on the bill: it sat on the calendar without a debate schedule, a committee referral, or a vote for the rest of the 112th Congress.

Separately, Congress attached a comparable 60-day decision deadline to the February 2012 payroll tax legislation; President Obama announced in January 2012 that the pipeline was not in the national interest, rejecting the permit while leaving the company free to reapply.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the pipeline came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, the President rejected the permit under the separate payroll-tax deadline, and oil sands producers and the pipeline company had to pursue a slower reapplication process rather than a legislatively forced approval.

for.name: Sen. Richard Lugar
for.role: Ranking Member, Senate Foreign Relations; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 30, 2011 and placed it directly on the Senate calendar, bypassing committee.

for.name: 39 Republican senators (cosponsors including McConnell, Murkowski, Hoeven, Vitter, Cornyn, Inhofe)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up 39 of the 40 cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democrat to do so.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Under a similar 60-day deadline enacted in the December 2011 payroll tax legislation, announced in January 2012 that the Keystone XL pipeline was not in the national interest and declined the permit.

against.name: Nebraska landowners and environmental groups
against.role: Grassroots opponents of the Sand Hills route
against.what_they_did: Rallied and lobbied against the pipeline route through Nebraska's Sand Hills and over the Ogallala aquifer, pressuring the State Department's review and Nebraska's legislature to force a route reconsideration.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 39 of the 40 cosponsors were Republicans, with only Senator Manchin of the Democratic caucus joining.

industries.note: The pipeline would have given oil sands crude a direct, high-capacity route to Gulf Coast refineries, supporting expanded production in Alberta. The bill's findings explicitly framed the project as locking in Canadian oil for US markets rather than Asia.
The pipeline company would have gained a legislatively granted permit and a route approved by default, with federal environmental review foreclosed.
Refineries along the Gulf Coast stood to gain a stable heavy-crude supply. Whether that translated into cheaper gasoline for consumers was disputed, since refined products trade on global markets.

industries.industry: Farmers and landowners along the route
industries.note: Nebraska landowners, particularly in the Sand Hills and over the Ogallala aquifer, had organized against the original route over spill risk to groundwater; the bill would have pressed ahead with construction while routing was reconsidered only on the state's terms.
